title: Keeping a Human Voice: Editing and Reviewing AI Content

production_notes: No facts to verify: examples are hypothetical and the lesson teaches a review method (content.md Review Flags: None).
Hira and the independent bookshop in Lahore are fictional. Stock footage must show no real bookshop name or logo.
Scene 3 generic phrases are quoted as examples of weak writing; show them in grey with a faint strike-through so they are not read as advice.

Hook.voiceover: In today's fast-paced world, it is more important than ever to. If you have read that sentence many times, you have already learned to spot unedited AI text. And so have your customers.

Explain.voiceover: Over the last four lessons, you created posts, articles, visuals and video with AI. Now we make sure they still sound like you, and are safe to publish. Unedited AI text often has signs that readers notice, even if they cannot name them.

slide.title: Keeping a Human Voice
slide.body: AI for Content Creators and Marketers · Lesson 10 of 15

Explain.voiceover: The first sign is generic openings, such as, unlock the power of. The second is repeated patterns, like the same sentence shape again and again, or every paragraph ending with a question. The third is claims without evidence, like proven, or loved by thousands. And the fourth is no specific details, nothing that could only come from your brand, your people or your place.

slide.title: Four signs of unedited AI text
slide.body: Generic openings ('In today's world…', 'Unlock the power of…') · Repeated patterns · Claims without evidence ('proven', 'loved by thousands') · No specific details

Explain.voiceover: When readers notice these signs, trust can fall, because the content feels like it was made without care. So use a five-point review checklist on every piece. Is it accurate, with every fact checked? Is it on-brand, matching your voice guide? Is it original, with something only you could know, and no copying or imitating of another creator or brand?

slide.title: The 5-point checklist
slide.body: 1 Accurate: facts, numbers, names, quotes checked · 2 On-brand: matches the voice guide · 3 Original: something specific to you, no copying · 4 Inclusive (next) · 5 Legally safe (next)

Explain.voiceover: Is it inclusive, with respectful language, no stereotypes, and captions or alt text so that different people can use it? And is it legally safe, with licences checked, permissions in place, disclosure that follows your rule, and no misleading claims? If a piece fails one point, fix it, or do not publish it.

slide.title: The 5-point checklist
slide.body: 4 Inclusive: respectful language, no stereotypes, captions and alt text · 5 Legally safe: licences, permissions, disclosure rule, no misleading claims. Footer: Fail one point → fix it or don't publish.

Explain.voiceover: Think of it this way. AI gives you clay. Clay has potential, but a lump of clay is not a finished pot. Your editing shapes it into something people recognise as yours. And your review is the firing that makes it strong enough to use.
Explain.stock_query: potter shaping clay pot on wheel

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's review a real draft. Hira manages content for a sample independent bookshop in Lahore, Pakistan. The shop is holding a poetry evening.

The AI draft says: in today's busy world, it is more important than ever to slow down. Join us for an unforgettable evening of poetry. Loved by thousands of readers, our events are the best in the city. Do not miss out.

slide.title: The AI draft
slide.body: "In today's busy world, it's more important than ever to slow down. Join us for an unforgettable evening of poetry! Loved by thousands of readers, our events are the best in the city. Don't miss out!"

Demonstrate.voiceover: Hira applies the checklist. Accurate fails, because loved by thousands has no evidence. On-brand fails, because the shop's voice is quiet, literary and welcoming, and the exclamation marks do not fit. Original fails, because nothing is specific to this evening.

slide.title: Checklist results
slide.body: Accurate: FAIL (red), 'loved by thousands' has no evidence · On-brand: FAIL, voice is quiet, literary, welcoming · Original: FAIL, nothing specific

Demonstrate.voiceover: Inclusive needs improving, because the post does not say whether the venue is step-free, and people often ask. And legally safe fails, because best in the city is a claim she cannot support.

slide.title: Checklist results
slide.body: Inclusive: IMPROVE (amber), add step-free access information · Legally safe: FAIL (red), 'best in the city' is unsupported

Demonstrate.voiceover: Her rewrite says: on Thursday evening, three local poets will read new work in Urdu and English, between the shelves where many of them first found poetry. Free tea is served. The shop is step-free. Reserve a free seat through the link in our profile.

slide.title: Hira's rewrite
slide.body: "On Thursday evening, three local poets will read new work in Urdu and English, between the shelves where many of them first found poetry. Free tea is served. The shop is step-free. Reserve a free seat through the link in our profile."

Demonstrate.voiceover: Hira explains her changes. She removed the generic opening and the claims she could not prove. She added the real details of the evening, and the access information. And she matched the calm voice of the shop.

slide.title: What Hira changed
slide.body: Removed: generic opening · unproven claims → Added: real details of the evening · step-free access → Matched: the shop's calm voice

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to edit only grammar and spelling. AI text usually has few errors of that kind. The real problems are generic language, unsupported claims and missing human detail. And asking a tool to make it sound more human is not enough. The real fix is your own specific knowledge.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, unedited AI text often shows generic openings, repeated patterns, claims without evidence and no specific details. Second, review every piece with the five-point checklist: accurate, on-brand, original, inclusive and legally safe. Third, the strongest edit adds specific human knowledge that only you or your brand have.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Spot the signs: generic, repeated, unproven, not specific. 2. Checklist: accurate, on-brand, original, inclusive, legally safe. 3. Add knowledge only you have.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below, review three pieces of AI-assisted content you made this week with the five-point checklist. Then rewrite the weakest one, and explain what you changed. It takes about thirty minutes. Next week, you build your capstone campaign. We start with the next lesson, Repurposing One Idea Across Channels. See you there.
